source: Mitchell, Russo, Pennington (1989) Back to the future: temporal perspective in the explanation of events
finding: The founding paper studied two factors: temporal perspective (event set in future or past) and uncertainty (event certain or not). Experiment 1 found temporal perspective had little influence on explanations. Outcome certainty strongly changed them.
numbers: Two experiments. Sure events gave longer explanations, more episodic reasons, more past tense. Experiment 2: uncertainty changed explanation type, not time spent. The Crossref abstract gives no 30 percent figure and no sample size.
quote: In the first experiment, temporal perspective showed little influence while outcome uncertainty strongly affected the nature of explanations for events.
limits: Only the abstract was read (via Crossref). The full text was paywalled, so the '30 percent more reasons' claim could not be checked at source. The abstract hints that the certainty framing, not the time shift, is the active part.
agent_relevance: The active ingredient to copy is 'treat the failure as certain', not a story about time. A prompt should state failure as fact.

source: Mitchell et al. 1989 as cited by Klein 2007 and others: the 30 percent claim
finding: A practitioner page says imagining an event has happened raises the number of reasons generated by about 30 percent, gives no N or statistics, and notes Klein (2007) words it differently (ability to correctly identify reasons, not number of reasons).
numbers: 30 percent; no N, no design, no quality rating of reasons. The page calls the academic literature on premortems thin and lists no direct replications.
quote: increases the number of reasons generated for the potential future outcome by approximately 30%
limits: Secondary source. The two wordings (quantity vs correctness) differ, so one of them is a drift from the original. Treat the number as unverified.
agent_relevance: Do not put '30 percent' into the schema as a measured gain. It counts as a hypothesis to test by counting distinct causes.

source: Implementation premortem article (2025) Proactive planning for contextual fit
finding: This paper repeats the 30 percent figure for Mitchell 1989 with no sample, design or baseline. It reports no controlled or comparative premortem study and calls published applications scarce.
numbers: No outcome numbers. Hill 2012 cited for reduced overconfidence, no figures. Brainstorming vs Nominal Group Technique (Mullen 1991 meta-analysis) cited without effect sizes.
limits: Secondary and by advocates. Says developer bias may persist after a premortem shows failure points. Whether it cuts real failure is stated as unknown.
agent_relevance: Even recent field papers rely on one old figure. Our test must be our own.

source: Veinott, Klein, Wiggins (2010) Evaluating the effectiveness of the PreMortem technique on plan confidence
finding: 178 students critiqued a university H1N1 lockdown plan. Premortem lowered confidence more than simple critique, pros and cons, or cons only. Seen only via summaries.
numbers: N=178, five conditions (per summaries). Confidence drop about twice that of pros/cons or cons-only (per jcx page). Exact means, SDs and effect sizes not seen. After generating solutions, confidence rose most in the premortem group.
limits: Original ISCRAM paper not opened (fetches blocked). Measured confidence and number of reasons, not plan success. One plan, one setting, students. Authors include the method's developer.
agent_relevance: The best-known test shows the technique shifts confidence. A lower confidence is only useful if it tracks real failure. For an agent, check change in answer correctness, not stated doubt.

source: Klein (2021) The pre-mortem method, Psychology Today blog
finding: Klein's own blog cites only the Veinott 2010 study as empirical support. It says premortem reduced overconfidence more than other critique methods, with no sample, effect size or method given. Other support is testimonials and media coverage.
numbers: No numbers. Method details: two minutes per listing step, failure imagined six months out (Pro-Mortem horizon about four years). Added steps (action for each problem, rating by likelihood, impact, ease) are untested.
limits: Author developed the method. Claims of better culture, trust and mental models cite no data. The Pro-Mortem variant is anecdotal.
agent_relevance: The evidence pile has a thin base: one lab study plus testimonials. Keep any pre-mortem operator behind a measured gate (G1).

source: Peabody (2017) Improving Planning: Quantitative Evaluation of the Premortem Technique in Field and Laboratory Settings (MS thesis, Michigan Tech)
finding: Three experiments. Exp 1: 52 Army cadets in teams ran six timed field exercises, half with premortem and half with the standard military plan review. Premortem teams had fewer fouls and less fixation, with no change in planning or execution time.
numbers: Exp 1 N=52 cadets, 6 exercises. Exp 2 N=72, premortem vs Worst-Case Scenario method on an engineering group plan: no significant difference in number of reasons or solutions. Exp 3 N=82: premortem gave more reasons than Worst-Case, and groups gave more solutions than individuals.
limits: Only the abstract page was opened; the PDF was blocked, so exact test statistics were not read. Unpublished thesis. Exp 2 is a null on counts against a close rival.
agent_relevance: A rival that also names failure (worst-case) can match premortem on quantity. The gain may come from asking about failure at all, not from the past-tense trick.

source: Peabody (2017) Exp 2 and 3 category distributions
finding: Premortem and Worst-Case Scenario prompts spread reasons across different categories. This suggests the two framings steer attention to different parts of the plan even when totals are similar.
numbers: Distribution of reasons and solutions across categories differed significantly in both Exp 2 (N=72) and Exp 3 (N=82). Exact chi-square values not seen.
limits: Abstract only. Category scheme is the author's own.
agent_relevance: Using two framings may widen coverage more than repeating one. Measure distinct cause categories, not raw count.

source: Gallop, Willy, Bischoff (2016) How to catch a black swan: measuring the benefits of the premortem technique for risk identification
finding: Journal of Enterprise Transformation 6(2). A controlled study of 101 program managers and engineers: premortem teams found significantly more quality risks than brainstorming teams (per the jcx page). Article text was blocked (403); only Crossref metadata seen.
numbers: N=101 (per secondary page). No effect size seen.
limits: Secondary report only. Counts risks, not later failures.
agent_relevance: A second source that premortem beats plain brainstorming on risk count. Same limit: counts, not outcomes.

source: Elizabeth (2020) SJDM poster: premortem, confidence and brainstorming (series building on Veinott 2010)
finding: A search summary says the poster compares a promortem with a premortem and tests individual vs group use. The group hypothesis was not supported.
numbers: No numbers seen. The poster fetch failed (connection refused).
limits: Search snippet only. Treat as a lead, not evidence.
agent_relevance: Suggests the effect is not simply stronger in groups. Check before assuming that more agents means more failure causes.

source: Aceituna (2019) PreHaz: premortem hazard assessment for autonomous vehicles
finding: Proposes narrowing the premortem search space by modelling domains that interact with the system, and deriving premortem questions from the overlaps. Worked examples only.
numbers: No experiment, no numbers.
limits: A method proposal, not a test.
agent_relevance: Open-ended 'what could go wrong' has no stopping rule. Structuring the failure space by interaction regions is a way to bound the search.

source: Wippold et al. (2024) Application of an implementation premortem (barbershop health programs)
finding: Qualitative premortem with 23 Black men: told the program had failed, they named failure sources and fixes. Main theme was program fit and accessibility. No outcome tested.
numbers: N=23, focus groups, coded with the EPIS framework. No comparison group, no effect size.
limits: Descriptive. Shows it produces themes, not that the resulting plan worked better.
agent_relevance: Failure stories from people near the setting surface real fit problems. An agent has no such people; its causes come from its own prior.

source: Psihogios et al. (2024) How to Save a Life: a premortem for pediatric digital health
finding: A one-time premortem with 14 professionals reached consensus on five failure themes. No test of whether the resulting plans did better.
numbers: N=14, one session, five themes.
limits: Convenience sample, commentary, no outcome.
agent_relevance: Typical of the field: many applications, almost no outcome tests.

source: Koriat, Lichtenstein, Fischhoff (1980) Reasons for confidence
finding: Classic root of the mechanism: asking people to list reasons their answer could be wrong reduced overconfidence, while listing supporting reasons did not (from memory of the paper).
numbers: Numbers not recorded this session.
limits: From memory; the abstract was not retrievable. Effect on calibration, not on accuracy.
agent_relevance: Gives a rival, older explanation: the benefit is generating contradicting reasons, which predicts a plain 'list reasons you may be wrong' prompt works as well as a premortem.

source: Matern, Baker, Saddawi-Konefka (2025) Consider-the-opposite debiasing in anesthesiology trainees
finding: A close cousin technique showed no compelling effect. Technical-skill self-assessment accuracy was unchanged; communication/leadership improved by 5.63 percent but missed the preset threshold for a meaningful effect.
numbers: Pretest-posttest. Technical: +1.00 percent accuracy (95% CI -7.46 to 10.0). Communication: +5.63 percent (95% CI 0.001 to 16.9).
quote: These findings do not suggest a compelling effect of this CTO intervention on self-assessment accuracy among trainees.
limits: No control group. Self-assessment of skill is not plan critique. Small trainee sample.
agent_relevance: A weak effect of a related 'argue against yourself' step. Boundary: the benefit is not universal.

source: Kaustia and Perttula (2012) Overconfidence and debiasing in the financial industry
finding: Field experiments on finance professionals: debiasing worked for better-than-average beliefs (written warnings, lectures) but only weakly for probability miscalibration.
numbers: Mixed results across overconfidence types. No figures in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Not a premortem.
agent_relevance: Overconfidence is several different things. A premortem may move confidence in a plan without fixing calibration of probabilities.

source: Rusmana, Roshayanti, Ha (2020) Debiasing overconfidence, KAAR model, Indonesian undergraduates
finding: Of the debiasing steps tried, watching a video about overconfidence was likely the most effective; an action-and-reflection part added less.
numbers: N=90, pre/post paired t-tests, five trajectory groups.
limits: No control group, students, not a premortem.
agent_relevance: Knowing about the bias helped more than doing a reflective exercise. Warnings may rival premortem.

source: Hao, Yu, Lou (2026) AUGUR: Proactive failure anticipation for reliable LLM reasoning (preprint)
finding: The only LLM paper found that calls itself a pre-mortem. A model is trained (not just prompted) to name likely failure points and verification steps before reasoning, then RL-tuned with a failure-anticipation reward. It beats GRPO baselines on math benchmarks.
numbers: Average accuracy gain over GRPO: +5.01 points (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), +4.28 (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), +5.66 (Qwen3-4B-Base). Benchmark names and per-set results not seen.
limits: Abstract only; full text blocked (403). Preprint, not peer-reviewed. Training method, so it does not show a prompt-only premortem helps. No ablation seen on pre-mortem vs plain extra reasoning.
agent_relevance: Shows the idea can pay when trained in. For our no-training scaffold, it does not settle the question.

source: Roose, Lehman, Veinott (2023) premortems in game development teams (as cited in the implementation premortem paper)
finding: Named in a citation with no findings reported. Listed as a lead for field use.
numbers: None seen.
limits: Citation only.
agent_relevance: Lead for a team-setting test; not usable as evidence.

source: Luth, Flinchbaugh, Crawford (2017) Help! My team failed: how conducting a premortem can improve group processes and outcomes (AOM Proceedings)
finding: A conference paper on premortems and team process. Crossref gave no abstract, so findings unknown.
numbers: None seen.
limits: Title only.
agent_relevance: Lead on group-process effects.

source: Huang et al. (2023) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: From memory: without external feedback, asking a model to review its own answer often does not help and can lower accuracy on reasoning tasks.
numbers: Numbers not recorded this session.
limits: From memory; not opened. Concerns post-hoc review, not forward failure imagination.
agent_relevance: Warns that an ungrounded 'imagine failure' step may add text without gain. Key to G2 and the signal-trigger rule.

source: Synthesis: what discriminates premortem from its rivals
finding: Rival explanations on file: (1) the certainty frame of the event (Mitchell abstract); (2) simply listing reasons against (Koriat 1980, memory); (3) worst-case prompts (Peabody Exp 2 found equal counts); (4) social permission to doubt (Klein). No experiment found that separates them.
numbers: No study seen that crosses certain vs uncertain failure with a reasons-against prompt.
limits: A synthesis of the sources above; no new data.
agent_relevance: For the agent: test 'certain failure' vs 'list how this could be wrong' vs no step, counting distinct causes and answer changes.

source: Absence of a meta-analysis or large replication
finding: In every source read, no preregistered replication, no meta-analysis, and no field trial with real plan outcomes was reported. The jcx page calls the literature thin; the 2025 paper reports no controlled outcome study.
numbers: Controlled outcome studies found: 0. Controlled confidence or count studies: Veinott 2010 (N=178), Gallop 2016 (N=101), Peabody 2017 (N=52, 72, 82).
limits: Search was limited: Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv were rate-limited and web search budget ran out. A study may exist that was missed.
agent_relevance: Treat premortem as unproven for accuracy. Keep it a gated optional check.

source: Peabody (2017) Exp 1 field result: fewer fouls and less fixation
finding: The one result tied to behaviour, not self-report: cadet teams using premortem committed fewer fouls and showed less fixation on the first plan, at equal time cost.
numbers: N=52 cadets, six time-limited exercises, premortem vs standard review. No p-values or counts seen.
limits: Abstract only, unpublished master's thesis. Cadets, game-like exercises.
agent_relevance: Equal-time cost is the useful point: a short check can fit a fixed token budget, matching our equal-token test.

source: Moderator: time and planning horizon (Peabody 2017; Klein method notes)
finding: Peabody extends the premortem to short planning horizons (timed exercises), where it still worked in Exp 1. Klein's method uses a two-minute listing step.
numbers: Short horizon tested in Exp 1 (six timed exercises). No dose-response across time lengths seen.
limits: No study varied the time allowed.
agent_relevance: A brief step is enough in people. Our token cost is the analogue.

source: Moderator: plan complexity and familiarity (Peabody 2017 Exp 3)
finding: Exp 3 used a complex, unfamiliar plan, and premortem gave more reasons than worst-case there, while Exp 2 (a simpler engineering plan) found no count difference. This hints that complexity moderates the premortem edge.
numbers: Exp 2 N=72 null on counts. Exp 3 N=82 premortem more reasons.
limits: Confounded: different tasks, samples and settings. A hint, not a test.
agent_relevance: Gate the step on task complexity or a signal of low confidence.
